author: René Descartes
title: Meditations on First Philosophy
length: 6 meditations plus dedication, preface and synopsis
openingChapterLabel: Meditation I — Of the Things of Which We May Doubt
openingText: Several years have now passed since I first noticed that, even from my youth, I had accepted many false opinions as true, and that everything I afterward built on such principles was therefore highly doubtful. From that time on I was convinced that I had to undertake, once in my life, to rid myself of all the opinions I had adopted, and to begin anew the work of building from the foundation, if I wanted to establish anything firm and lasting in the sciences. But the project seemed so large that I waited until I had reached an age mature enough to leave me no hope that any later stage of life would find me better fitted to carry out my design. For this reason I have delayed so long that I would now think myself in the wrong if I went on consuming in deliberation any of the time that remains for action. Today, then, since I have happily freed my mind from all cares [and am happily disturbed by no passions], and since I am in the secure possession of leisure in a peaceable retirement, I will at last apply myself, earnestly and freely, to the general overthrow of all my former opinions.
about:
What can you know with certainty if even your senses can mislead you? Across six meditations, Descartes asks whether human knowledge can have a secure foundation. He begins by setting aside his previous beliefs. Dreams can resemble waking experiences, and perhaps even what seems obvious could be deception. Yet while he doubts, he cannot deny that he exists as the one who is thinking.

From there he attempts to prove God's existence, explain human error and establish that a physical world exists. He argues for a real distinction between mind and body while also describing their close connection through pain, hunger and thirst. Follow both his arguments and the objections he raises against them.

The work appeared in Latin in 1641. This edition contains the dedication, preface, synopsis and six meditations. The Objections and Replies to which Descartes refers are not included here. The book is short, but its arguments build on one another and reward slow reading.

angleCards.title: What can doubt show?
angleCards.text: Descartes uses doubt to search for certainty. Notice why he questions the senses and then even what seems mathematically obvious.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the stages of doubt and identify precisely what each puts in question.

angleCards.title: The first certainty
angleCards.text: In the Second Meditation, Descartes discovers that he must exist while he thinks. Ask what this certainty tells him about himself and what it does not yet establish.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand why doubting cannot cancel my existence while I doubt.

angleCards.title: Mind and body
angleCards.text: Descartes distinguishes the thinking mind from the body that occupies space. Yet he also experiences them as closely joined. Read for both sides of his account.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how Descartes distinguishes mind from body while also explaining their union.

angleCards.title: God and certain knowledge
angleCards.text: God has a crucial role in Descartes's account of certainty. Notice the difference between clearly seeing an argument now and later remembering that you understood it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how the proofs of God and the rule about clear and distinct perceptions support each other.

cast.name: René Descartes
cast.description: Descartes develops the arguments in the first person and invites readers to think them through themselves. The preface asks for attention to their order and connection rather than to isolated famous sentences.

cast.name: Methodical doubt
cast.description: Everything open to doubt is provisionally set aside. The aim is certain knowledge, not permanent doubt about everything. Dreams and possible deception make the test more demanding.

cast.name: The evil spirit
cast.description: At the end of the First Meditation, Descartes imagines a powerful deceiver trying to mislead him. This is a supposition that sustains the exercise of doubt, not a claim that such a spirit exists.

cast.name: The cogito
cast.description: The name is often associated with 'I think, therefore I am.' In the Second Meditation, Descartes establishes that 'I am, I exist' is necessarily true whenever he thinks it. This does not yet establish an external world.

cast.name: The real distinction
cast.role: The different natures of mind and body
cast.description: In the Sixth Meditation, Descartes argues that he can clearly conceive mind and body separately and that God can therefore make them exist separately. He also contrasts the body's divisibility with the mind's indivisibility.

cast.name: The question of circularity
cast.description: Descartes uses clear and distinct perceptions in proving God and invokes God to guarantee their truth. Readers can ask whether this reasoning is circular. The Fourth and Fifth Meditations invite attention to the different roles of present attention and memory.

whyItMatters.title: Examining certainty
whyItMatters.body: The book distinguishes feeling convinced from being able to justify a conviction. Readers can test which reasons might withstand even far-reaching doubt.

whyItMatters.title: Experience and explanation
whyItMatters.body: The piece of wax, dreams and pain in an amputated limb make abstract questions concrete. These examples explore the difference between what we experience and what we infer from it.

whyItMatters.title: Following a sustained argument
whyItMatters.body: The six meditations let readers follow a justification across several stages. You can accept one step while still asking whether the next follows. That makes the work an exercise in careful, critical reading.
